In other words, In 1906 there will be an average of ten trains a day of thirty cars each for every day in the year, and in 1911 fifteen trains of thirty cars each for every day in the year. We can see what this means when I say that, according to the last census, for three years the average had been about 120 cars per day, or four trains of thirty cars each for every day in the year. In other words, in 1906 we ought to have two and a half times as many train loads come out, and in 1911
nearly four times as many carloads of these products of the North-west Territories coming out that we have to-day. Now, lion, gentlemen opposite, and the leader of the opposition amongst them, have pinned their faith to the advantages of lake and rail transportation as against all-rail transport.
Hear, hear.

The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) says, ' hear, hear.' I have no doubt he pins his faith to that of his leader, whatever it may be. Nevertheless, though the leader of the opposition pinned his faith to water and rail transportation, he proposes to provide for all-rail transportation and many hon. gentlemen on the other side have discussed that very favourably. The argument in favour of water and rail transportation is supported almost entirely by statements in regard to the transportation of wheat and wheat alone, upon the fact that wheat may be carried by lake and rail more cheaply than it can be carried all-rail. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition, in the course of his statement of programme announced that he favoured the acquiring of the Canadian Pacific Railway track from Sudbury westward to Fort William, and then nationalize the track from Fort William to Winnipeg. This must be for the purpose of providing an all-rail route and shows that the hon. gentleman appreciated the importance of that route, and sees that the water and rail route is not sufficient for the needs of our transportation. I can quite understand, if the hon. gentleman depends on the Canadian Pacific Railway line north of Lake Superior, that the argument that the all-rail route cannot compete with the lake and rail route has a good deal of force, because everybody knows the impossibility of the Canadian Pacific Railway north of Lake Superior competing with the lake and rail route. We are all aware of the fact that that railroad has grades on it of one per cent; we are all aware of the fact that, spend as much money as you like upon it, do what you choose to improve that road you never can make it, from the nature of the country through which it is going to pass, a portion of a great transcontinental railroad which can and ought to carry freight at the lowest possible figure.
But, Sir, 1 will take the hon. gentleman's contention that we must have a lake and rail route. Nobody on this side of the House objects to that route during a portion of the year, in summer. But I want to point out this, that while grain alone, and especially wheat, will probably be carried when the lake and rail route is available, chiefly by the lake and rail route, wheat is not by any means the only product that will be carried I out, in fact is not the greatest product that,

in the near future, will have to be carried out from the North-west. My hon. friend from Peel a few moments ago alluded to the argument of my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior about the carriage of cattle into the North-west Territories from the east by this railroad route. My hon. friend perhaps is not aware of the extent of that trade. This last season over 25,000 head of store cattle were carried from eastern Canada beyond Lake Superior into the Northwest Territories, for the purpose of supplying that country with stock; and my hon. friend is not aware of the fact perhaps that at the same time there was no less than
40,000	head of cattle came from Mexico into our North-west Territories. Why V Because there was not a convenient route by which to take them at a low rate from eastern Canada into the North-west. Now, Sir, I venture to say that while the 25,000 head that went into the Northwest Territories last year and an almost equal number that went in the year before, came largely from the province of Ontario, in the near future the maritime provinces and Quebec, and even that northern country through which the Grand Trunk Pacific transcontinental road is going to pass, will be able to raise young cattle which can be profitably taken into our North-west Territories for the purpose of being fattened there and then sent back to the east to be exported to the mother land. My hon. friend shakes his head. Perhaps he forgets the fact that during the last few years we have been sending from eastern Canada into the states of the American west thousands of cattle for the same purpose. My hon. friend perhaps does not know that although the western states of the union have been the greatest cattle producing country in the world, notwithstanding that fact, buyers from the western states, from Iowa, Missouri, Kansas, Colorado and Nebraska, have been scouring the Dominion of Canada to get store cattle to take into the western states to be fattened there and then sent east to Chicago, to be re-exported to England. Now, Sir, if that condition of affairs obtains in the cattle industry of the western states of America which have been developing it for years, may we not expect that in the North-west Territories of Canada, as their cattle trade develops, the same thing will obtain.
The hon. gentleman says that the export of cattle from Canada to the Unites States is increasing. Can he give us the figures for the last three years V

No, the trade has not been increasing. Why ? Because our own people have wanted all their cattle to reproduce in this country, they have been refusing to sell them to the Americans because they have found a new Hon. Mr. FISHER.
market for them in our own North-west. That is the reason why our cattle trade has been increasing. But it is not because the western states do not want them, it is not because the western states are not getting^ them, but to-day the western states are getting their store cattle from Mexico just as our people in the North-west are doing', because they cannot get them in Canada: and it is only because they cannot get them in Canada in sufficient quantity that they have been turning their attention to the south and they are getting them from Mexico.
But the hon. gentleman has entirely supported the view which I am expressing to the House. The hon. gentleman is quite right when he says that in the near future the people in the North-west will breed cattle for themselves. They are doing it to-day, and they are going to do it much more in the future. It is just as important, and indeed more important for the development of our North-west, that the cattle and stock industries should be developed than that wheat should be raised. The people of eastern Canada know well that the live stock interest is the basis of their prosperity. They know also that those people who have gone from eastern Canada to the North-west and Manitoba, while for a few years they do without live stock by reason of the virgin fertility of their soil and the ease with which they can raise great crops of wheat on the fertile prairies, in the near future they will have to adopt what is known as mixed husbandry and establish a live stock interest. When they come to do that the amount of animal products which they will want to send out of the North-west Terri-tornes will make the amount of wheat that is sent out pale into insignificance in comparison. Sir, we are going to have in Canada the same condition of affairs in the development of our North-west that the United States republic has had. When the people from the east went into that country and began to spread out over the Mississippi plains and further west, they began to raise wheat and corn. They afterwards took to raising cattle to such an extent that to-day Chicago is the centre of a far greater trade in animal products than it is of a wheat and flour trade. I venture to predict that while to-day the people of Manitoba and the Northwest are thinking of hardly anything else than wheat and flour, they will in the near future devote their attention to the animal industry in the shape of packing houses, in the shape of abbatoirs, in the shape of a live stock trade, which will cause the grain trade of our North-west to sink into insignificance. When that time comes, as it surely will come in the near future, no part of that trade in animal products will go by lake and rail but the whole of it will be obliged to go by rail, and can go in no other way. I emphasize this fact, because in all the discuss-

ion of the transportation question, not only-in this House but in the newspapers of the country, the problem has been held to hinge upon the grain trade, in comparison with which everything else seems to be considered of no importance.
I have some figures here which will show what the trade of Chicago is in reference to this matter, and I think we may fairly judge of what is going to happen in our own country by what is happening in the United States. Winnipeg is held to be the future Chicago of our country. Chicago is situated at the head of lake navigation. Winnipeg is nearly 500 miles away from lake navigation. If there is any place on the continent of America where lake transportation can advantageously compete with all rail, it is Chicago. When anything has to be sent from Chicago to the Atlantic seaboard it can only go by lake to Buffalo, and then rail from Buffalo, or by the Erie canal with only one transhipment, or it can go all rail from Chicago to the Atlantic seaboard without any transhipment at all. Now, anything that comes from Winnipeg-and Winnipeg must be in the future the centre for the gathering of all the products of our great North-west- anything that comes from Winnipeg, if it has to come by water as well as by rail, will have to come down to Lake Superior before it can reach the water. It will then have to be transferred into the ship, be brought down to some other point and there it will have to be transferred again either to the rail at the G-eorgian bay ports, or into the ocean vessel at the port of Montreal, or at some other of the seaports. In that respect water and rail transport is at a less advantage from Winnipeg than from Chicago. But, what is the fact as regards the transportation of the products of the west from Chicago ? I have some figures taken from the Chicago Board of Trade returns which show how the products of the great west whicb are assembled at Chicago go to the Atlantic seaboard. I fear I may weary the House-
Go on.

In 1900 grains, including wheat, corn, oats, rye, barley, grass and flax seeds to the amount of 3,449,000 tons were sent from Chicago eastward by the water route, and grains amounting in quantity to 2,287,000 tons were sent eastward by all-rail. There were of flour alone
109.000	tons sent by water and 614,000 tons sent by rail. I will now take animal products. including barrelled pork, bacon, dressed beef, hides and wool, lard, cheese and butter, not live animals, but only animal products. By water there were sent
20.000	tons from Chicago to the east and by rail there were sent 1,445,000 tons. If you
take the three things together, grain, flour, and animal products, there were sent from Chicago eastward in the year, 1900, 3,579,000 tons by water and 4,347,000 tons by rail.
Is that from Chi-cargo to the seaboard direct ?
Yes, direct.	'
Not all to the seaboard ports ?

Not all to the seaboard ports. The return only shows what went eastward without specifying that which went to the seaboard, but the great bulk of it went to the Atlantic ports. This calculation does not take into account the shipments of the enormous quantities of grain which go through Chicago south and east and do not enter Chicago at all but which are sent straight on without any delay. The return which I am quoting are returns only of what goes to Chicago and is sent on from there and that which goes to south Chicago goes on by all-rail. I venture to say that there are ten times as much of these_ as of the quantities which I have given which do not go to the Atlantic seaboard. In 1901, taking the figures from the same source, we have of grain alone, 2,169,000 tons going by water and 2,439,000 tons by rail. We have of flour 89,000 tons going by water and 724,000 tons going by rail the whole way. We have of animal products 15,000 tons going by water and 1,444,000 tons going by rail. This shows clearly and distinctly that the arguments which might be brought up in detail, a little here, and a little there in the course of this debate, are not conclusive in favour of the water and rail route. I think this statement is a direct and complete answer to the statement made the other day by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) in his speech, when he said, quoting the words of a rail expert :
Not more than ten per cent of the wheat is caried by the rail route and it is so carried only in times of necessity when it is absolutely necessary to bring the grain forward at almost any cost. In the United States the rail and water routes carry over seventy-five per cent of the grain in the United States and it must be remembered that the rail competition there is over railroads which run through a thickly populated country having large commer [DOT] cial interests.
Sir William Van Horne is quoted as saying that not a single bushel of the grain can be carried along the north shore of Lake Superior.
I do not think Sir William Van Horne said that.

I do not know but it would be the most severe condemnation of the route of his own railway that could possibly be brought before this country and it would have no bearing whatever upon the argument on this question because the grades on the route which we are proposing are doubly as good as the grades along the north shore of Lake Superior on the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Is it settled what the grades are to be ?

It is settled to this extent: We know that the grades of the Canadian Pacific Railway around the north shore of Lake Superior are as high as one per cent, and we know from the statements which are made in regard to the country through which this proposed road will go that instead of it being an extremely rocky and hilly country with high elevations and deep ravines, it is generally level country with a gradual slope the whole way, and I am informed that the Grand Trunk surveying parties who are now in the country have been able to secure as far as they have gone a route with grades as low as one-half per cent, or in other words, that it is double as good as the route of the Canadian Pacific Railway around the north shore of Lake Superior in the matter of grades. That is one of the weaknesses of the proposition of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, because, in comparison with the route which we propose, the proposition which he puts forward cannot compete with the lake and rail transport and will not be able to do so. If we are going to provide facilities for transporting the grain products of our North-west we must provide for the construction of a
railway which can and will be able to successfully compete with the lake and rail transport, and the proposition which we have put forward will do that, and I believe that no other proposition which can be brought forward will be able to do it.
Now, Sir, I will allude to another fact in connection with the argument put forward a few minutes ago. I said that not only wheat and grain, but also animal products from our North-west must be brought forward. I will turn to the report of the Winnipeg Board of Trade and point out that in that report they draw attention to the remarkable fact that last year the Minneapolis millers obtained a concession from the United States government by which they have been able to get Canadian grain and grind it in bond for export to Europe. The board of trade says : that apparently the result was satisfactory, as it has been announced in the press that a large quantity of the Manitoba wheat of this season's crop has been shipped to Minneapolis millers for grinding. That means that a large proportion of the Canadian wheat crop, instead of being exported to Europe in the shape of grain, is being ground into flour by the enterprise of our neighbours to the south, and according to the statement of the Winnipeg Board of Trade they are making a profit out of it. Is it not reasonable to suppose, yea, is it not necessary to the proper development of our western country that our own people at Winnipeg, Rat Portage and other places in the west, shall grind the wheat of western Canada in flour, and send it as flour to the eastern parts of Canada as well as for export. I know that to-day the reason why so much wheat is brought from the west into eastern Canada to be ground into flour, is because there is no market in the North-west for the byproducts. The people of the North-west have not yet got into the way of feeding bran and middlings and shorts to their cattle and hogs, but when they get to be a live stock-producing country in the Northwest, and have an abundant market for the by-products of the wheat when it is ground into flour, then you will see in Winnipeg or somewhere else another centre like Minneapolis where to-day the wheat of the western states and of Canada as well, is ground into flour ; you will see the erection of enormous flour mills, and the products of our western plains will be shipped to the east in the shape of flour instead of in the shape of wheat. When that comes about, the flour will come from the west to the east by rail, and little or none will be shipped by the water and rail route. ^ Here we have another proof that an all-rail route is absolutely necessary. And that all-rail route must be the best possible one. The kind of route "which the leader of the opposition has spoken of will not do. He proposes to have it along the north shore of Lake Superior where the grades are

most difficult, and through Ontario and Quebec in a roundabout way, in contradistinction to the straight road proposed by the government, which will go through the hinterland from Winnipeg to Quebec in the most direct way. The leader of the opposition proposes to do this by buying the Canadian Pacific Railway around the north shore of Lake Superior; by purchasing the Canada Atlantic Railway; by building a long link ; and by improving the grades by some arrangement between Port Arthur and Winnipeg. The leader of the opposition presents to parliament a patchwork scheme, presents to parliament a patchwork plan, which will not accomplish the end desired, of a straight road with low grades and a direct course between two important points. The leader of the opposition proposes to carry out his plan by an expenditure of tens of millions of dollars; I do not know liow many tens of millions. He himself said that be did not object to free expenditure, and I must say that his plans show that he seems to delight in expenditure.
An lion. MEMBER. It would cost hundreds of millions.

It may, but I am not able to go into a detailed calculation at the present moment, although we know that the cost would be enormously greater than the cost of the government plan, which the Finance Minister has stated to the House and to the country will only cost us 813,500,000.
Some bon. MEMBERS. Oh.
My hon. friends opposite laugh.
So well we might.

Do they laugh at the figures brought forward by the Finance Minister ? Let me tell them that neither in this House nor anywhere else in the country has a single figure ever announced by the Finance Minister been controverted or attempted to be controverted. More than that, in the seven years that my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Fielding) has held the position of Finance Minister, he has year after year put before this parliament and before the people of Canada financial statements, and they have all been of so conservative a character that in no single instance have hon. gentlemen opposite been able to point to any error or misstatement in his calculations.
Hear, hear.

Yes, the reputation of the Finance Minister is so high in Canada that the people of Canada will accept his statements and will feel absolutely sure that the price which the_ hon. gentleman puts upon this great project is the outside figure it will cost the people of the country. I venture to say Hon. Mr. FISHER.
that never in the history of Canada has any plan of such transcendent importance been submitted to the people that involves such a mere bagatelle of a burden upon them.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The Minister of Finance found it hard to get money enough to pay the cost of taking the census.

The Minister,of Finance has been able, during the last year, to show to the people of the world that the revenue of Canada is so abundant that we have a larger surplus by double than ever was known in history before, and that notwithstanding the hon. gentleman's insisting upon the fact that the census has been expensive.
I do not wish to enter into the general terms of this debate. The question has been dealt with ably by gentlemen on both sides, and I compliment gentlemen opposite that they have put their best foot foremost and given their ablest and severest criticism to the plan of the government. But all they have been able to show is that the plan of the leader of the opposition has not the full concurrence of the gentlemen behind him. These gentlemen opposite have recognized that the hinterland must be developed and that Canada should be widened from north to south so as to get a firmer grip on our area for agricultural operations. The leader of the opposition states that he is willing to build a colonization railway from Quebec to Winnipeg. He is quite willing to do that after having spent millions after millions in acquiring the Canada Atlantic Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway on the north shore of Lake Superior and improving the grades on the Canadian Northern Railway or the Canadian Pacific Railway from Lake Superior to Winnipeg. And after all these millions have been spent, he is willing to build a colonization road from east to west.
When ?
In his speech.
At what time does he propose to do it ?
Just as soon as the information can be obtained and as the information is now before the House and the country, no doubt the leader of the opposition wants to do it at once.
When the interests of the country demand it.

The hon. gentleman from Peel said that plan would not do, and the hon. gentleman from Jacques Cartier said that it would not do either, and that you did not want a railway from Quebec to Winnipeg, but that you wanted colonization roads to be run

from the old settled parts everywhere to the north. There is not the slightest doubt in the world that such roads would not develop the country as the plan which the government proposes. The plan promulgated by these gentlemen will not afford good and cheap transportation facilities for the products of the western country, but the plan which the government has proposed will without doubt render that blessing. By this plan we propose to give to that part of Quebec and Ontario one of the best railroads on the continent of America, a road which will be on the main line of our communication between the great west and our seaports on the Atlantic; a road which will be able to carry the products of our western country at the cheapest possible cost, and will, therefore, promote the colonization of that country to the best advantage. As I have pointed out, the hon. leader of the opposition proposes to a great extent to follow oifr lead. But his followers do not believe in his scheme ; they want to build the road in a totally different way. Sir, we make a clean-cut proposition embodied in a contract signed and sealed with a reputable corporation of great resources, which is going ahead with the project as rapidly as possible. In opposition to that and in contrast to that, my hon. friend the leader of the opposition proposes a scheme which involves dickering and bargaining with three or four railway corporations, each of them with its hand on the throat of this country, so that if his party were in power they would be committed to this scheme, and would be obliged to yield to their demands. We do not know, we cannot know, what that will cost. We do know, and the country knows, what our scheme will cost, and tiie cost is so ridiculously small that the difficulty is for the people to believe that so much can be got at so little cost.' But, as I said a moment ago, the people of this country have had experience of the work of the Minister of, Finance, and when he tells them, that this scheme can be put through at a cost of $13,500,000, they will believe him, and .will support and vote for the scheme. I for one, shall be glad to go before the people of the country and ask for their endorsation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this late stage of the debate, I would not have ventured to occupy the time of the House were it not that the importance of the subject makes it the duty of each one of us to pronounce upon it. Tiie hon. Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher), who preceded me, promised that he would give us some new points to excuse
this scheme which the government are forcing upon the country; but in the course of the hon. gentleman's argument, I found that he was not dealing with the transportation question at all, but was giving us some very interesting figures about the development of the agricultural products of the west, and the bright prospects of that country for the future. I am sure that we are all very glad that the North-west is going to have the great future which we all predict for it ; but that has nothing w-hat-ever to do with the transportation question. The hon. minister quoted figures which in themselves, may be all right and proper ; but they had nothing to do with the issue before us on the present occasion. They show the real need of deliberation on this question. The hon. gentleman pointed out that in ten or twenty years hence the products coming out of the North-west would be enormous. That is all the more reason, Mr. Speaker, why we should pause now to get the right solution of the question of how to bring these products out by the cheapest outlet. But the hon. Minister of Agriculture is a docile follower of his leader, and therefore he did not wish to trench on the poor excuse which the right hon. leader of the government gave for bringing this project before the House, but contented himself with damning the whole scheme with faint praise. After telling us that the waterways afforded tiie cheapest outlet for the transportation of the products of our western country, he -went on to excuse the project of a railway to supplement them, without developing any comprehensive scheme by which our water-ways could be improved.
Now, this question of transportation is the most important question that can come before this parliament, in view of the place commercially which Canada is to take in the future amongst nations of the world. We have reached a stage in the history of the development of transportation in all parts of the world, that should cause us to pause and deliberate before we commit this country to a project which will probably keep hack the true solution of the transportation question in this country for years to come, and possibly place the country financially in a position that would put her capability of coping with this question and her ability to carry as cheaply as the United States entirely beyond our reach for an indefinite period. The struggle for supremacy in international trade continues at the present time in all its vigour. It is recognized in all commercial countries that that struggle is one of the foremost issues that confront them to-day. Not only is our international trade bound up in this transportation question, but the whole internal development of the country is involved in it. If Canada is going" to take commercially her place among the nations of the world, it is absolutely necessary that

the country should have transportation facilities equal if not superior to those of the nation to the south of us. Undoubtedly we are not prepared for the solution of this question at the present time. It is not without grave and thorough deliberation and ample knowledge, gained from all sources, that we can hope to find a solution of this question. This was the position of the government at the opening of the present session, for we find in the speech from the Throne these words :
The whole question of transportation and terminal facilities continues to occupy much attention, and my government will immediately appoint a commission of experienced men to report on the subject.
This shows the position of the government at that time. It shows that they were not prepared to deal with this question without having expert opinions upon it. Five months have since elapsed, and have we got that commission yet ? Mr. Speaker, I believe that not one member of that commission has been appointed, and no report on the subject has been brought in by the government. If further evidence were necessary, we have only to refer to the Order in Council passed on the 19th of May last, and subsequently brought 'down to this House, which contains some very interesting statements, in view of the project now before the House. This Order in Council has been read by several hon. members, but I think it is a good thing to bring it once more before the promoters of this scheme. The members of the cabinet apparently had a pretty comprehensive idea of what should be done in order to arrive at a true solution of the transportation problem. This Order in Council states :
That the development of North-western Canada has manifested the inability of existing Canadian transportation agencies to take care of Canadian products.
That our agricultural exports can only command the prices over seas to which their natural excellence entitles them when they cease to be confounded and confused with the inferior and often adulterated articles produced elsewhere ; and to preserve their separate Identity they must go through Canadian channels.
The minister further states that the questions to be considered are complicated and involved, including among the conditions to he sought the transportation of western products from place of production to the markets of the world.
It appears to me that with a statement of that kind, an acknowledgment by this government that expert opinion should be had in order to thoroughly investigate the different phases of this question, it is premature and ill-considered to bring down a scheme to this parliament three or four months after the opening of the House. The Order in Council goes on :
It is obvious that before any satisfactory conclusion can be reached upon these questions a thorough and comprehensive inquiry should he made regarding :-

The conditions of original shipment and the possibilities of improvement in the conditions surrounding such shipments.
The storage requirements of lake, river and ocean ports.
The harbour facilities of the inland lakes, rivers and Atlantic and Pacific ports.
The conditions with regard to the navigation of the St. Lawrence route, and, generally, any improvement, enlargements, of other matters affecting the more economical and satisfactory uses of any Canadian channel of transportation by land or water.
The minister further states that In making such investigation attention should not be confined to routes and facilities which are at present utilized, but, if necessary, new surveys should be made to determine whether any more economical and satisfactory channels of transportation by land or water can be opened up.
The forces operating against the attainment of all-Canadian transport, namely :-
Competition by United States railways;
Competition by United States vessels from Lake Superior ports;
Diversion of Canadian products through eastern outlets to Boston, Portland and other United States ports, should be investigated, and the best and most economical methods used by our competitors should he carefully studied and reported upon.
The minister apprehends that in these circumstances it devolves upon the Dominion government to consider and adopt the best possible means of promoting such measures as may enable Canada to control the transportation of Its. own products, and it is thought that the most efficient method of conducting such an inquiry and obtaining the required information is by means of a commission of competent and experienced experts who may he appointed and authorized under the provisions of chapter 114 of the Revised Statutes of Canada.
Now, it would not be supposed, having this view at the opening of parliament, having enunciated this view and having brought it down to the House on the 19th of May, that this government would plunge into a scheme of this kind without having any thorough or well-considered plans, surveys or Information to present to this House.
The hon. the Minister .of Agriculture -said that this was not introduced hastily, that the country had really been considering it for two years. Well, if the country has been considering it for two years, how-is it that the government had not a scheme to present to this House at the opening of parliament ? How is it that they brought in these different resolutions and finally at a very late period of this session brought in the present scheme. The minister quoted the Winnipeg Board of Trade to help out-his argument, but what do we find the Winnipeg Board of Trade saying :
That a thoroughly qualified expert In the management of railways be appointed to make a report on existing conditions, and what, in his opinion, would make the Intercolonial a paying concern and of the greatest benefit to the country, and also to study and make recommendations on the following alternative schemes for the consideration of the government and the people.
The hon. minister apparently forgot to

quote that part of the recommendation of the Winnipeg Board of Trade. But we have not only this resolution, we have further the opinions of a man whose life has been devoted to railroad and transportation questions, and who, I believe, was asked to take the chairmanship of this proposed commission, a man who has pronounced against this scheme as a means of solving the transportation question of the west. Sir William Van Horne spoke as follows :
The Canadian Pacific Railway, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, or any other all-Canadian route will never voluntarily carry a carload of wheat by the all-railway route around the great lakes to an eastern Canadian port for shipment abroad, for the simple reason that It will never pay any road to do so. Nor will the transportation problems in the west ever be solved by the construction of an all-Canadian route from coast to coast.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this House and the country well know the reputation of Sir William Van Horne. They know his connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway, and they know very well that if any means could be devised by which the Canadian Pacific Railway could carry their grain to the eastern ports over their own line, they certainly would not use lake transportation.
One might also say that we have the opinion of another man who is considered perhaps an equally good authority on the transportation question in the estimation of hon. gentlemen opposite, the manager of the Grand Trunk Railway, Mr. Hays. When this scheme was first brought forward the Grand Trunk Railway had no idea of building a transcontinental railway through from coast to coast via Quebec and Moncton. Their idea was to go in by Grav-enhurst or North Bay in order to tap the wheat fields and to establish their line in the North-west Territories. Why the government departed from this and adopted this last scheme, by what means they were pushed into this, is beyond my comprehension, unless it was to satisfy the call of their political grafters. The ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair), who, among the members of the government, had the widest experience in connection with railway matters, and to whom one would naturally suppose his colleagues would look for information and guidance on this question-why was he not taken into their confidence at an early date, and why were his opinions not listened to ? We find that this minister, whom we naturally should have looked to. leaves the government because he does not agree with this scheme as a solution of the transportation problems of the west, and in a masterful and well-considered speech which up to the present time has not been answered by the government or its supporters, absolutely condemned this proposed scheme. But it seems to me that we do not even have to point to such high authorities as I have mentioned for the
condemnation of this scheme in the light of the experience of one hundred years of the transportation problem in the United States. The scheme is condemnatory in itself. There is indeed not one point of merit in the whole scheme to recommend it. It is true that the right hon. the Prime Minister announced that it was designed for two purposes. First, to transport grain from the west to the seaboard ; and, second, to protect Canada in case the bonding privilege should be taken from us by the United States. In all fairness, except from this announcement it must be said that one would not judge that it was designed for any such purpose, but rather that some ulterior object was to be served in running a line into the country where for years to come there will be absolutely no traffic to warrant such an expenditure. Surely we have never had a scheme proposed in the history of legislation in Canada which was supported by such weak and flimsy arguments as those which were advanced by the hon. the leader of the government. The bonding privilege ! The hon. the leader of the House grew eloquent over the fact that the bonding privilege was going to be taken from us : the commercial advancement of Canada was to be stopped if we did not devise some means of freeing ourselves from dependence on the bonding privilege. Let us look for a moment at the annual report of the Inter-State Commerce Commission of 1S92, about the time that the fears of the hon. the leader of the government were awakened in this regard. The report says :
The ' foreign transit trade ' has also been a great mutual benefit to the two countries. The statistics indicate that the ' foreign transit trade ' of Canada through the United States is very much greater than that of the United States through Canada, hut that the reverse Is the case as to the ' domestic transit trade ' of the two countries. The charges for freight per train mile on the Intercolonial Railway is only 98 cents compared with the $1.51 on the Grand Trunk, while the operating expenses are a great deal less on the Intercolonial Railway than on the Grand Trunk. And the freight rates over the state-owned lines on the continent of Europe are very much lower than are those on the English railways which are owned by private corporations.- The Intercolonial Railway, mile for mile, is equipped equally well with the Grand Trunk, though It has only half as much traffic, and its operating expanses, including the maintenance of the line, buildings, &c., would not be greatly increased by an increase in [DOT] the traffic. At very little additional expense that road could handle double the traffic that it has at the present time. The possibilities of this road under proper management, if it were placed in the hands of a commission independent of politics would be greatly improved. During the jrast seven years we have spent upwards of $15,000,000 on the Intercolonial Railway, all with a view of extending it westward in order to reach the wheat fields of the west. But now it is proposed to spend $100,000,000 to undo the work of the past seven years, and prevent the realization of the objects which the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) with the approval of his colleauges has been striving to attain since he first had the honour of holding the portfolio of Railways and Canals.
Now, as to the cost of this project, it is variously estimated at from $120,000,000 to $150,000^000. And I believe that one gentleman, the lion.' member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) who has had a great deal of experience in railway matters, says that the cost will be upwards of $280,000,000. That is, he points out that during the first twenty-five years' operation of a railway, the improvements that are necessary double the original cost. Suppose that this railway cost originally $120,000,000, it will double
in the first twenty-five years of operation to $240,000,000, and, at the end of fifty years we shall find the cost nearer $500,000,000. To put a moderate estimate on the present cost of the road, the figures will come out in this way. Estimating the eastern section from Winnipeg to Edmonton at 1,800 miles, and $40,000 a mile, we have $72,000,000 for that section. Interest for ten years at 3i per cent would be $25,200,000, and the difference between 3 per cent and 3i per cent for forty ears, $12,640,000. For the mountain section, interest on bonds for tern years $7,200,000. This makes a total of $117,040,000. This does not take account of interest that should be legitimately charged to capital account for the time the road is building-or probably $4,000,000 or $5,000,000 more. Then there is the guarantee on the bonds which will easily put an incumbrance on the credit of Canada of $30,000,000. or $40,000,000. Besides which we have the Quebec bridge which will probably cost the country some $5,000,000. So that the estimate with which the right hon. First Minister tried to mislead the House and the country, that the cost of the road would probably be only $13,000,000, is absurd. The Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher) is the only member on the other side who had the temerity to say that this estimate of $13,000,000 was a ridiculously low one. But as I said before, the Minister of Agriculture is a docile follower of his leader.
Now, I do not want to trespass on the time of the House, nor do I want to trench on any provincialism in connection with so vast a problem as this. But, since the leader of the House has brought down a project that has no inherent good qualities ns a transportation system to recommend it to the country as a whole, as this is evidently a project to serve the political purpose of hon. members on the other side and their friends, and is giving additional rail facilities to every province at confederation except Prince Edward Island, I think I may fairly ask why Prince Edward Island has been left out of any consideration, and would say just a few words for railway needs in Prince Edward Island and in support of the proposition brought down by the hon. member for West Prince (Mr. Hackett) some time ago, and voted down, that we should at least receive some consideration in the way of transportation facillities in Prince Edward Island. On this point I am quite ready to agree with the right hon. leader of the House and say that this is a time for action and not for deliberation. There has been long, long deliberation in the case of improving transportation facilities in Prince Edward Island, and now we want action. As this House knows, we have been labouring under a great disability in regard to transportation between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. I do not want to enter again into a history of the terms of

confederation, but it is well known that the Dominion government bound itself to provide continuous steam transportation between the island and the mainland, winter and summer, thus putting the island in direct communication with the railway system of Canada. Now, that the transportation question is the uppermost in all our thoughts, and now that the government is trying to satisfy all the other provinces, it seems to me that something should be done to satisfy the legitimate requirements of Prince Edward Island. I have already pointed out the deplorable condition of affairs last winter by which a large number of our shippers lost heavily and which loss I trust this government has seen the justice of redressing. I do not wish to present a large array of figures on this question, but it would be easy to show the great disparity between the treatment meted out to Prince Edward Island and that meted out to other provinces with regard to the expenditure on transportation facilities since confederation. Take this scheme that is now before us. Prince Edward Island will be obliged to contribute one-fiftieth part of the expense. That will amount to somewhere in the neighbourhood of $2,000,000. The railway in Prince Edward Island was built entirely at the expense of the province, being charged to us at confederation at a valuation of $3,144,214, or an average of $32.50 per head of the population. Since that time there has been spent in public improvement on the island $1,485,090. But only one small branch to Cape Traverse has been built until the last year or two, when the branch was built to Murray Harbour. Now, Mr. Speaker, we in Prince Edward Island have not been getting our fair proportion of railway improvements. This was recognized by the late Conservative government, but unfortunately too late to remedy, and this government, although urged repeatedly to build branches to meet the requirements have turned a deaf ear and now suggest an immense scheme, touching all the provinces of confederation, but absolutely ignoring the most pressing needs of transportation with Prince Edward Island and mainland and the railway branches in several parts of the island much more thickly populated and whose needs are more pressing in order to open up unknown territories with unknown resources.
I have on several occasions brought forward the necessity of a branch from North-Wiltshire to Crapaud and there are lines of equally pressing necessity in western parts of the island-namely at or near O'Leary station to west shore of the island.
All we want is fair reasonable treatment, and while not objecting to any reasonable scheme and expenditure for our great and rapidly growing west we want to keep in mind our older provinces.

When you take into consideration the fact that out of $4,629,304 spent in Prince Edward Island, $3,144,214 was paid for by Prince Edward Island, or charged against her at confederation the comparison is odious, so small has been our portion. The Cape Traverse branch was built with a view to offering some relief by maintaining transportation across the strait in winter as well as in summer.
But the government has seen fit to abandon us, and we are very much in the situation that we were when we entered confederation in this regard. Now that they have at their disposal means and opportunities of relieving the situation, they ought to put us in direct communication with the railway system of the Dominion of Canada, and for this purpose they could well acquire the New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island Railway, leading from Sackville down to Cape Tormentine. They would then have only seven or eight miles to cross by steamer, and, as I have pointed out several times in this House, it is the natural and shortest route between the island and the mainland as an alternative route when the ports of Summerside and Charlottetown are not available. If they would put on a proper steamer at these points, if they would give us more facilities, facilities for which the people have been petitioning year after year by making a pier and affording landing facilities on the island side, they would do a great deal to relieve the transportation problem in Prince Edward Island.
But transportation is not our only grievance. There is the matter of telegraphs, about which we have been petitioning this House, and in respect of which the government is under obligation to provide us a reasonable service. We have down there a company that has been claiming to possess a monopoly of the situation, and has been charging us exorbitant rates, while only giving us a twelve-hour service. This question came up the other day in a committee of the Senate, and it was clearly pointed out that no monopoly existed, and the Senate, in reply to an amendment brought forward by the attorney of the Anglo-American Company, asking that right to establish a cable be not granted the Dominion Telephone and Telegraph Company's Bill, threw out the amendment and virtually

declared that no monopoly existed. It remains now for this government to act and provide us an up to date service.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have pointed out what I consider the means at the disposal of this parliament for solving the transportation question of this country. As I said at the beginning, it is an all important question which will put Canada in the foreground as a commercial nation. We should utilize our great water-ways, and we should supplement those water-ways with the most easy and natural means to reach our ocean ports. The scheme outlined by the leader of the opposition presents, as I said, a comprehensive and easy method, and I trust that the government will yet pause in its mad career and consider this question anew.

I agree with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lefurgey) who has .iust taken his seat that it would be almost impossible to offer anything new on this subject, and in view of the great accumulation of information that we have before us. it would be perhaps in vain to attempt to add anything to it. As you and I, Sir, generally sway the opinions of others in the House, and as you, I believe, are go-1 ing to form your own judgment in regard to this question, permit me to remind you that we have been exhorted by my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) to approach this subject in a judicial manner. In order to do that, I would suggest that we should, first of all, determine for ourselves what has been proved and admitted on this question. In the first place, it is proved that it is the duty of the country, as represented by the government, to assist the North-west. What was the condition of Manitoba ? We have been told that there was an accumulation of produce, notably of grain, and that the people of that province had no facilities for obtaining the full value of their products by taking them to market at a reasonable cost. Who advocated the railways ? Who represented that condition of the country ? The gentlemen who represent public opinion in the North-west. The press complained of the accumulation of produce, the members from Manitoba in this House represented truthfully that the inhabitants of that territory were sadly injured by the lack of proper facilities, and the House believed the testimony that was given on their behalf. Now, Sir, the government-assuming this to be correct, and there has been no one to gainsay it, no one to refute it-agreed that to provide for the present and future there should be some facility for relieving that accumulation of produce and benefiting the people who inhabit that territory. They agreed that that facility should be the shortest, the best and most economical means of transportation between the west and the east, in the form of a transcontinental railway. In the second place, as the cost of furnishing this facility is great, and as the
whole country has to contribute to the payment. it is admitted to be right and proper that all the provinces of the Dominion who contribute to the accomplishment of that desired end should participate in the advantages accruing from the transport of the produce of the North-west and should share in the benefits of the productions of that land. In addition to that, it is provided that the carriage of these commodities should end at our own ports. Therefore, in view of these considerations, we have the government proposing to build a railway from Moncton to Winnipeg and to aid in the construction of a railway from Winnipeg to the coast. Let us see whether this proposal accomplishes the ends we have in view, and whether the cost will be too great in proportion to our resources.
I have taken the liberty of suggesting that that facility should be a railway, and I do it with great deference to my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island who has just addressed us .and for the following reasons: First of all, that a canal is a very expensive work. Secondly, it is unfortunate that we have no rivers flowing from that country, and that the construction of a very expensive work like a canal, where there is no water in the country, does not afford much facility for the carriage of produce. Against this proposal what does the opposition contend ? Among other things, they contend, firstly, that the government cannot economically build the road. I might ascribe the assertion of that proposition to my hon. friend from Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart). Secondly, that the government will not build the road. I think, on the other hand, we may safely attribute the defence of that proposition to my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker). Thirdly, that the government will build the road at an enormous cost. Without any hesitation whatever, I think the House will attribute the sponsorship of that proposition to the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule). Fourthly, that the Grand Trunk Pacific will not operate the road, that traffic will not go over it (a) from natural causes : (b) by some great treachery on the part of the government; (c) by some hocus pocus on the part of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway ; and, fifthly, we have the proposition of the hon. and learned leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax).

We had a speech in this debate by the ex-Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair), and another by the ex-ex-Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Hag-gart). As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, 1 entertain the highest respect, and I may say almost admiration for the ex-Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair). His conduct in this House; his mastery of the details of business; the successful manner in which he has piloted railway legislation through the House command our admiration and respect. I have no desire, even if I lut'd the ability, to belittle in the slightest manner or to the slightest extent the reputation of the hon. gentleman. I only regret that he has left the government at this time when his experience and services would be most valuable to the country in assisting in the passage of this most valuable measure. But although the ex-Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) was a most valuable administrator of railways, I possess no knowledge of his ever having constructed a mile of railway, and although his opinion as an operator of railways would be perhaps as valuable as almost any administrator, still on a question of the location, or the construction, or the practicability of a railway, I would prefer to take the evidence of an engineer, or of one who had to do with the practical construction of a railway. Now, Sir, we are not at a loss for the opinion of a railway engineer of eminence, Sir Sandford Fleming, the most celebrated engineer in Canada, or perhaps in America, who has just completed the great project of a Pacific telegraph cable from Canada to Australia, and who has an intimate knowledge of the whole of the country to be traversed by the trans-Canada, was interviewed by a reporter when
it was announced that the Grand Trunk Railway contemplated building a transcontinental road. His opinion, which follows, is a remarkable confirmation, by the greatest known authority, of the wisdom of the selection of the route provided for In the Trans-Canada charter :
I am inclined to think Mr. Blair is on the right track in proposing to extend the Inter-colnial Railway to the Pacific. It seems to me, however, that it would he a mistake to try to form a new transcontinental line in a haphazard way by connecting various fragments of railway which have been located without any general plan. The effect would be to lengthen the whole line and unduly lower its engineering character, and almost certainly give it features which would be for ever regarded1 as blemishing to a great transcontinental line. To realize Mr. Blair's conception of a new national railway, it should, in my judgment, begin at the Quebec bridge, now building, where it would form a direct connection with the Intercolonial, and it should extend from Quebec by the most direct route to Port Simpson on the Pacific. Prom what I know of the general character of the greater part of the intervening distance I believe a line with splendid engineering features cculd. with ordinary care, be secured. It would pass away to the north of the rugged shore of Lakes Huron, Superior, Nepigon, and Winnipeg, through a vast region reported generally of alluvial soil, with abundance of wood and water.
First-The Quebec bridge is in progress, that structure I have always favoured, hut it would have been a bold man to have proposed such a work a quarter of a century ago. The Quebec bridge will give the needed connection with the Intercolonial as well as the Grand Trunk Railway, and along with a junction with these railways access and egress to and from Atlantic points at all seasons
Second-The greater part of the vast region through which the new line might pass between Quebec and Port Simpson is woodland, and we have ta-day a new value given to the timber, which was undreamed of twenty-five years ago. The territory to be traversed is the natural home of pulp wood, and in this vegetable substance the unoccupied regions of Quebec and Ontario have an inexhaustible crop ready for harvesting. A crop of a perennial character, which, in extent, I venture to say, Is unsurpassed in the North American continent-perhaps in the whole world.
I have already expressed my doubts as to the wisdom or expediency of proceeding in a haphazard way to establish a new transcontinental railway. I regard the. shortest line obtainable between the tide-waters of the two oceans as quite long enough. For that and other pogent reasons I would advocate the most favourable route which can he had between the port_ Quebec and Port. Simpson for a new Dominion Grand Trunk line, and at the same time to have in view the establishment of railway service with all desirable points by branches judiciously laid out. By having regard to these leading principles, great advantages would, ^ in my judgment, result. It seems to me there is ample room for the new railway. It would in no way interfere with any other line, and it may he regarded as a natural development of the railway system of Canada. I am satisfied that it Is possible to establish a splendid national railway on the route proposed with the best ocean ports at its terminal. With a Rocky Mountain 1 passage very much lower than that of any

railway yet constructed across the North American continent, and with general engineering features even more favourable than those obtained on the Intercolonial Railway, such a line would give breadth to Canada and admit of settlements and profitable industries where such are not now possible. In the far Northwest it would open up for ranching the rich plains of .the Peace river and Northern British Columbia, and render the more distant gold fields more easily accessible at all seasons.
When the day arrives to open the railway as a through route it will be found to possess advantages, in respect to distances, as compared with the route via San Francisco and New York. From Yokohama to Liverpool the passage across the Pacific ocean would he 605 and across the Atlantic 195 nautical miles less. While the land distance would he 502 statute miles less, making a total saving on the whole distance of about 1,423 statute miles.
Regarded simply from a Canadian standpoint, I cannot conceive any public undertaking which would better meet the wants of the New Dominion, throughout its whole extent. I rejoice to know that it has so soon in Canadian history been brought up for serious consideration.
That is the opinion of Sir Sandford Fleming, and my friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Lefurgey) is to the contrary.
The next gentleman who attracted our attention in this debate was the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, my hon. friend from South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart). Although my hon. frien'd was supposed to have had great experience in the construc-Ion of canals, his experience In the construc-lon of railways was quite as limited as the experience in that respect of the ex-Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) ; and although I cannot compliment him in the same terms as I can the ex-Minister, on the economical and satisfactory administration of his department, I must admit that his experience In the operation of a railway is far greater than his experience in the construction. But I have often admired my hon. friend. He comes into this House charged with the subject upon which he is going to speak, and he employs all his vehemence and positiveness of manner. When he is right, he is irresistible ; he bears down on his opponents like a frigate with all sails set. and guns out on both sides. I am free to admit that when he is wrong-and he is wrong very often he is equally positive, and if possible more vehement; he will not listen to any reasons to the contrary; and, by vociferation, assertion and obstinate adhesion to himself, though he is in the wrong, he hears down all opposition, and comes out triumphant in the end. My learned friend, tile regulator of the opposition, sent to my hon. friend and called him to come to this House to curse Quebec and defy Nova Scotia, and he carried out that request with the utmost circumspection. He took up his parable like the prophet of old ; and, when he began to curse Quebec and to defy Nova Scotia, he turned his face to the wilderness, and what did he say ? He said that a railway through that country was positively impracticable ;

that it was a region utterly unfitted for a railway to pass through ; that it was rough; that it was full of jungles, abounding in muskegs, and traversed, by granite ridges throughout its length. Well, a gentleman who has passed through that region declares that this is one of the reasons why people in a certain state of mind are subject to hallucinations. This is what is said by Mr. O'Sullivan, who was employed by the transcontinental railway people and the government of Quebec to survey that region during the winter of 1897-98 :
During the winter of 1897-98, I left a party at Rupert House who surveyed the shore line and the estuaries of, the rivers In that locality, and in March and April traversed in a direct line across country from Rupert House to Lake Abitibi, imd thence homeward via Lake Temis-caming. A, proof of the favourableness of that country for railway construction, no obstruction of any kind was encountered on this traverse, but an optical illusion was often experienced, for in the morning when they would strike an open plain, they would perceive ahead of them what appeared like mountain ranges in the distance at right angles to their course, but continuing their march day after day without changing course they never came to them- it is all a gently rolling plain.
If the government should send out their surveying parties-and they will send them out-and if they should find geysers, uphill torrents, glaciers, crevasses, serbonian bogs

That difficulty was apparent throughout the course of his speech because after he had criticised the proposition of the government, after he had denounced it, after he had found fault with it, he took it up piece by piece and in detail and he,told us that he approved of most of the parts of it, that is that he was ready to give his support to any proposal which would give a better fighting chance to the lower provinces; that he would help by his vote to assist in the consummation of the desired results, but he would not support this proposition. My hon. friend in the course of his remarks asked : What will the government do with its 1,600 miles of Intercolonial Railway; and how much of it will be used V He was speaking in answer to the argument of my hon. friend from Hants (Mr. Russell) who had addressed the House on the subject of government ownership of railways, and he said :	If you do away with the
