Now, Mr. Speaker, the people of Canada have made great sacrifices in order that the provinces may be bound together and a great Canadian nationality built upon this north American continent. When it was agreed that Nova Scotia and New Brunswick should confederate with upper and lower Canada, a part of that agreement was that the Intercolonial should be constructed at the expense of the new Dominion. And the Dominion of Canada made great sacrifices to construct that road. At a later period, the province of British Columbia came into the confederation, one of the terms of the arrangement being that the Canadian people should construct a line of railway across the continent in ten years. At this time it became known to the best informed of our people that we had a splendid heritage in the North-west. Many of our farmers were flocking to the prairie lands of the western states in order that they might find cheaper lands for their children. The fact presented itself to the minds of the Canadian people that it was necessary to open our western country so that the people of the older provinces, instead of going to a foreign land, would be able to find cheaper homes for their children under the flag beneath whose folds they were born. And, with this consideration in view, the government of Canada went to work to construct a line across the continent. In 18S0, or 1881, the government entered into a contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to construct this line in ten years, for which the company were to receive 25,000,000 acres of land, $25,000,000 in cash, and that portion of the road which was constructed or under construction, which cost the people of Canada $34,000,000. In all, the Canadian Pacific Railway cost the people of Canada $84,000,000. And the people at that time felt that they had made a great bargain. It was a great undertaking for the company to build that line across the continent. The hon. gentlemen opposite had magnified the financial burdens to be borne in constructing this road. They said it would cost $300,000,000, and the picture they gave of British Columbia and the north-western country, of which they now speak so highly was enough to dampen the ardour of the people of Canada. It is no wonder, therefore, that

when the government found a company ready to construct a road on these terms, the people felt that a great burden had been taken off their shoulders. We all felt that the government had made a great bargain. And I think that that is borne out by the fact that the first $25,000,000 of Canadian Pacific Kailway stock that was placed on the market only brought twenty-five cents on the dollar, while the whole $85,000,000 of stock realized only $50,000,000. The people who invest their money in these stocks are the best judges of the merits of an enterprise of this kind. There were a few people at the head of affairs who had confidence in Canada, who had confidence that the road would ultimately pay. The result was that the Canadian Pacific Railway was constructed not in ten years, but in six years. In 1886 the first train passed over the road to Vancouver. And, Sir, after seventeen years of operation of that road what is the result ? The gross earnings of the Canadian Pacific Railway last year were no less than $43,000,000, a larger sum than the money received for customs throughout the whole of Canada. The $85,000,000 of Canadian Pacific stock which had been sold for $50,000,000 in the market of the world, was worth, a few months ago, no less than $125,000,000, or $75,000,000 more than was paid for it in the first instance. This company for years has paid on its common stock no less than 5 per cent, and this year it is declaring a dividend of 6 per cent. I say that the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway was one of the greatest financial achievements in our history, in fact it was the greatest financial success ever achieved in this country. 1 say that if the people of Canada supported the construction of a road under these conditions, I ask why should the people of Canada to-day, with the different conditions, with trade waiting for the railway, a trade which must make the road profitable from its inception, be called upon to saddle themselves with an expenditure of from $150,000,000 to $250,000,000 in order that we may have a fresh batch of multi-millionaries at the expense of the people ? I would present this as the strongest fact, the fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway has been a great financial success, and that the conditions for railway construction and operation are much more favourable than they were. The company constructing a road across the continent to-day will find it a profitable undertaking if they never receive a dollar from the people of Canada. The fact that the people of Canada assisted in building a railway for the purpose of cementing the provinces and uniting the Canadian people, as well as to develop sections of the country at that time unopened, is no reason why we should be called upon at this late day to add this immense sum to our national debt in order to construct a railway to which these reasons cannot apply.
Now, I should like to say a few words with regard to this eastern division. I know that a great many figures have been plac'd before the House, but I have my own ideas, and my own opinions, which I desire to state. In my opinion, whatever justification there may be for constructing the road from Winnipeg westward, there is positively no justification for constructing the road from Winnipeg to Moncton. I believe it is a waste of the people's money. And we have the statement of the ex-Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) to the effect that the road from Winnipeg to Moncton will cost from $70,000,000 to $75,000,000. In making up his estimate of the amount, that hon. gentleman did not take into consideration the interest on the money during construction. Then we are to pay interest on this indebtedness for ten years after the road is finished. Then we hand it over to the Grand Trunk Pacific, and they pay us 3 per cent for the balance of the period of fifty years. There is something about this agreement still more unsatisfactory. When I first heard of the contract, I was under the impression that the earnings of the whole line would be placed under contribution to pay the interest of 3 per cent on this section, which is the lean and unprofitable portion of the road. But I find that this agreement does not carry that out, that only the earnings of the eastern section, the unprofitable section, are taken into consideration when they pay this 3 per cent. That is, we have the unprofitable end, we have constructed the eastern division; and there is no railway expert in Canada will tell you that the eastern division in 25 years will earn its working expenses. Set this is the portion of the road that we expect to receive 3 per cent upon after it has earned its working expenses.
There is another feature in connection with this matter more disagreeable still. After having built this road and handed it over to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for 50 years, according to this agreement we have to pay everything for the betterment of that road, and we do not know where this expenditure is going to end. Everything for the betterment of that road must be paid for 50 years by the people of Canada. I ask you to go back and look at the Intercolonial, a railway which originally cost this country $21,000,000. Inside of 15 years, the betterments of that road, everything in the way of permanent improvements. had cost more than the original construction; and railway men everywhere say that in ten or twelve years after the construction of a road the betterments, or the permanent improvements put on it, will cost quite as much as the original construction. Now, this line of railway from Winnipeg to Moncton is to cost this country $75,000,000 at first; then, according to the precedent of the Intercolonial, it will cost us $150,000,000. and we are handing this road over to the company to operate it

without the least prospect of ever receiving a dollar in return. I ask you. What is there to warrant such an expenditure as this ? We are sending out settlers to a country which can never become a desirable country to live in. A few may exist there, but it must for ever remain an unattractive country for settlers so long as we have these fertile lands in the North-west; and I ask you why should we send our people up among the jack pines, the spruce and the birch in northern Quebec or in northern Ontario, while there are millions of acres of fertile prairie lands in the west open for settlement ?
Now, Sir, I wish to say a few words as regards the probability of this road ever being able to relieve the congestion in the west. If there is anything in connection with the construction of this line that must affect every ratepayer in Canada, it is that this eastern section never can by any means carry the cereals of the west to the seaboard. The distance from Winnipeg to Port Arthur is 425 miles. We have two lines of railway, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern, both stretching from Winnipeg to Port Arthur. Both have low gradients and small curvatures, both are in a position to carry an immense number of cars loaded with grain, at the least possible cost. This is proved by the action of the government of Manitoba, who, on gaining control of the Canadian Northern, immediately fixed the rate of grain from Winnipeg to Port Arthur and from the west to Winnipeg, at the lowest possible cost to the farmer, so that in the shipment of his grain lie would receive as much as possible after deducting the cost of carriage. I think this is the best evidence that the amount that is charged for carrying grain from Winnipeg to Port Arthur is the least rate at which it. it is possible that the grain can be carried. Now, Sir, to-day they are charging twelve cents per 100 pounds, and I understand that on the 1st of September they are going to try to carry that grain for ten cents per 100 pounds, equal to about six cents per bushel from Winnipeg to Port Arthur. If it costs ten cents per 100 pounds to carry grain from Winnipeg to Port Arthur, a distance of 425 miles, and I have shown that is the least rate at which it can be carried over that distance, I ask you what will it cost to carry 100 pounds of grain from Winnipeg to Quebec, a distance of 1,600 miles ? It is true that by a straight line it is 1,400 miles, but if you add ten or fifteen per cent for curves, you get 1,600 miles as the shortest distance that it will work out. Well, now, if it costs ten cents per 100 pounds from Winipeg to Port Arthur, at the same rate over the 1.600 miles, it will cost just thirty-six cents per 100 pounds, or twenty-three cents per bushel. Now, the cost of'carrying a bushel of grain from Winnipeg to Montreal by rail and water haul is only about eleven cents per bushel-eleven cents Mr. THOMSON (Grey).
against twenty-three, or a difference of twlve cents. If the farmers of the west were to ship 100,000,000 bushels of grain over this road which the government propose to build, it would cost them $12,000,000 more than by rail and water. Do you think a farmer is going to pay twelve cents more to ship his grain over this road than he could ship it by rail and water route ? Not by any means. He will hold his grain till navigation opens. We are told this road is only to carry grain when navigation is closed. But do you mean to tell me that after navigation is closed the farmer of the west will sell his grain for twelve cents less in order that he may ship over this special line to be constructed by the government ? No, he will borrow the money on his grain, and he will hold it until spring in order to save twelve cents a bushel. I think that is clear as noonday. I do not hink that grain ever can be shipped over this road, and if this road is being built in order to afford the farmers relief, it will prove to be a perfect failure.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words in support of the splendid policy which has been enunciated to this House by the leader of the opposition. It is quite evident that the leader of the opposition has given a great deal of study to this problem; I have no doubt that he has also had the assistance of experts in the preparation of this scheme. Let us look at this problem for a moment. He tells us that we can acquire the Canada Atlantic Railway. Remember that the Canada Atlantic Railway to-day is a paying institution. If we purchase the Canada Atlantic Railway we have got an asset that is .worth the money that we pay for it. Now, if it is paying to haul grain from Depot Harbour to Coteau, I >ask you : Would it not be equally profitable to carry grain from Depot Harbour to Montreal by all-rail ? I see no reason why we could not acquire running powers over the Grand Trunk railway from Coteau to Montreal, and then we would have a railway from Montreal to Depot Harbour, which will prove the very best security and a paying road. In addition, this proposition extends the Intercolonial from Halifax to the foot of the great lakes, which will make the Intercolonial Railway a much more valuable property than it is to-day, while it would not cost the people of Canada one copper. I say that this is a masterly, a splendid proposition, and I ask you to compare it with the scheme of running a road up through northern Quebec and northern Ontario, a distance of 1,600 miles, in order to canny out the grain of the west.
My hon. friend stated that if the policy of the hon. leader of the opposition were adopted : the extension of the Intercolonial Railway to the foot of the great lakes, what freight would it haul ? He did not know that there were over 29,000,000 'bushels of grain shipped from the lower ports

of the Georgian bay last year and that this year the quantity will be still greater. If we acquire the Canadian Pacific Railway from Sudbury to Port Arthur what position are we in? That has been an expensive road and we will require to spend more money to put it in proper shape, but when we have purchased that road we will give running powers to the Grand Trunk Railway, to the Canadian Northern to the Canadian Pacific Railway and to the Intercolonial Railway and the receipts or rentals from these companies having running powers over the line (because it would be taxed to its fullest capacity where it has now but one-tenth of the business it could do) will pay the interest charges, and the road is ours. The House will remember that the proposition of the hon leader of the opposition was that these roads should acquire running rights over the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific to Winnipeg and they will have to pay for them. What is the use of hon. gentlemen opposite dealing out figures as to the cost of the scheme which has been proposed by the hon. leader of the opposition V The only cost that would be the cost of acquiring these roads and when we have acquired them they are ours and they become a paying property the moment we have acquired them. This proposition if carried into effect would tremendously enhance the value of the railway property of the people of Canada. It would give the Grand Trunk Railway Company immediate access to the wheat fields of the west. The Grand Trunk Railway has a magnificent network of railways, a splendid railway property in Ontario and Quebec. There is not a dty, town or village of any importance in the province of Ontario that it does not touch and hon. gentlemen can imagine the importance it is to this line to have immediate access to the wheat fields and carrying trade of the west. If the policy propounded by the hon. leader of the opposition were to go into effect to-morrow the stock of the Grand Trunk Railway would advance fifty per cent in thirty days. This is the scheme worthy of the traditions of the Conservative party and we are proud of the traditions of the Conservative party, which, as the hon. leader of the opposition has said, is the party that had the heart to construct the Intercolonial Railway and to construct the Canadian Pacific Railway which have done so much for the development and consolidation of Canada and it is the party that is prepared to solve this difficult problem that is before us to-day. I ask the right hon. leader of the government to appeal to the people on this question. Let the people have an opportunity of expressing their views and I believe if such an opportunity is given them it will be the best thing that could be done in the interest of Canada to-day. If the right hon. gentleman does not appeal to the people
he should at least abandon the scheme and thereby save the honour and national credit of Canada.
